As a teenager, David Durman would read works by Enlightenment philosopher David Hume and the Stoics. Their ideas led him to adopt the Humanist faith, a nontheist system he said centers human well-being and flourishing, which he’s kept for 30 years.

Because Humanism’s emphasis is on moral responsibility for one’s choices, the now 45-year-old administrator at the University of Kentucky felt uncomfortable by the “growing normalization” of AI products and systems at work, where colleagues and leadership offered “mounting suggestions” of how to use the tools and floated the idea of going to conventions to learn more about AI. For Durman—who disables Gemini on his Google searches and generally disables as many AI features as he can—surrendering any tasks to the technology chafes against what he sees as the goals of his faith.

“To me, the offloading of any decision-making capacity or ability to interpret the world around you—including what’s true, what’s not true, what’s going on with the world—reduces your ability to act towards those goals,” Durman told Fortune.

While the University of Kentucky doesn’t yet have an AI directive, Durman said he wanted to preempt “any work environment move towards an actual requirement.” In August, he filed an accommodation request under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act —which protects religious views and nontheistic ones—to the university to be exempt from AI usage with the help of his attorney Alexandria Huiskens, who works with the American Humanist Association.

“When David reached out to us, I think we were both in agreement that we see AI as potentially displacing human judgment, reason, responsibility,” Huiskens told Fortune . “A lot of Humanists don’t realize that they can approach their employer with this kind of exemption or accommodation, so when David reached out, I was thrilled.”

The University of Kentucky arranged a meeting with Durman and Huiskens, in which they discussed the sincerity of his views, and then granted his request on Sept. 25, determining that accommodating his beliefs under Title VII didn’t impose an “undue hardship ” on the institution. Employers face a higher bar for denying religious accommodations since the 2023 Supreme Court ruling in Groff v. DeJoy , which established they must show accommodating an employee’s religious observances would impose substantial costs to their business rather than minor inconvenience.

“My exemption doesn’t apply to other employees, and I’m not trying to affect other people’s work,” Durman said.

Durman’s exemption comes as employers push workers to embrace AI despite growing anxiety about the technology. Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke has called AI use a baseline expectation, while Amazon urged software engineers to adopt it when useful. More workers are using it, but also fear falling behind if they don’t. A Gallup poll found 52% of U.S. employees used AI at work at least a few times a year as of May 2026, up from 21% in 2023. At the same time, an American Psychological Association survey this year found 37% of workers worried about falling behind colleagues if they didn’t use AI, while 48% feared it could make some or all of their job duties obsolete.

Durman also isn’t alone in raising moral objections to AI use. Pope Leo XIV notably warned in his May encyclical that relying on AI could erode human creativity and judgment and called for more oversight, referring to AI as “ a valuable tool that requires vigilance .”

Durman said he was aware of the Pope’s encyclical and even read parts of it, but wasn’t necessarily influenced by it in his accommodation request. He was more inspired by Erin Maus, a software engineer and practicing Unitarian Universalist who got a religious exemption from using AI at her tech company in May.

But Durman’s exemption doesn’t mean any employee opposed to AI can refuse to use it. For Title VII’s hardship standard, the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Office distinguishes sincerely held religious beliefs from personal preferences and political or economic views. Huiskens said Durman’s decades of Humanist adherence and his efforts to avoid AI in his personal life helped establish his case. Whether another employee could pull off the same request would depend on their beliefs and the impact on their employer.

“That’s kind of up to these larger corporations and or universities to comment on and make a determination on,” she said. “Right now, we are just reacting to what we are seeing and making sure that our members and Humanists generally are protected.”

OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team, moving its researchers onto other teams. The company confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune. A company spokesperson said that robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision and portrayed the reorganization as a sign of the company’s commitment to robotics, rather than a retreat from it. OpenAI said it has reassigned its robotics research team to the company’s main research team, reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams have been reassigned to the company’s larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman. The change came recently enough that OpenAI had already registered a booth at CoRL, a top academic robotics conference in Austin, this week. Though the conference app and floor plan marked OpenAI’s spot, when Fortune visited booth #208, it sat empty with OpenAI’s logo nowhere to be seen.

OpenAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI)—the human-like AI that has been OpenAI’s goal since its founding—through other methods. In particular, OpenAI became increasingly devoted to training ultra-large language models on vast datasets of human-written text. This is the approach that eventually yielded the company’s breakthrough product ChatGPT in late 2022. OpenAI rebuilt a stand alone robotics team in 2024, announcing a partnership with the startup Figure to develop AI models for humanoid robots. That partnership ended in February 2025, when Figure said it would develop its own robot AI. OpenAI has said it is currently developing its own humanoid robot, with CEO Sam Altman targeting a first public demonstration in 2027. The company spokesperson said that despite the reorganization, OpenAI remains committed to bringing general-purpose robots into the world. The reorganization reflects a bet that is gaining traction across the AI industry: that general-purpose models built for language, code, and vision can also be used for “embodied AI”—where AI models control devices that can act in the physical world, such as robots, driverless cars, or drones. This would obviate the need to have separate robotics teams building specialized AI models just to be the digital “brains” for robots. Researchers have seen surprising performance when connecting GPT-6 Astra to robots, directly using the general-purpose AI model to perform some robotic tasks. Guanya Shi, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, reacted to the change at OpenAI, telling Fortune that he would interpret the move as a signal that OpenAI sees robotics as “no longer a special problem.” Instead, he said, they likely see robotics as a challenge that can be addressed as a downstream application of general intelligence—similar to the way the same underlying frontier AI models now power specialized coding tools, or tools for legal or financial work. OpenAI seemed to confirm this view in its response to Fortune. It said that at the start of the year, the company’s researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on AI models such as Sora, a video generation model that, in order to create realistic videos, had to have some implicit understanding of how the physical world works. But since then, the company spokesperson said, the company’s general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown that can be directly applied to robotics. This discovery is what motivated OpenAI to disband the stand alone robotics team and move the affiliated researchers onto teams working on more general AI models. The reorganization also comes at a time when OpenAI is under pressure to rein in its costs and show that it is more focused on a few, core products. Last year, Altman told the company that it needed to abandon “side quests,” and the company has jettisoned some efforts—including Sora—in order to reallocate computing resources to more core and potentially-profitable endeavors. The company is under pressure to stanch its heavy operating losses—which reportedly totaled $10.9 billion in the most recent quarter—as it seeks to close a new funding round and prepares for a possible IPO in early 2027.

This line of thinking—that general AI models can be applied directly to controlling robots without the need to create specialized models with “spatial intelligence”—would seem to challenge the assumptions underpinning many of today’s robotics startups, which have raised billions on the premise that robots need brains of their own.

But Russ Tedrake, an MIT professor and cofounder and CEO of Walden Robotics, said robotics companies still have an advantage the AI labs don’t: Their robots are already gaining work experience in real places, such as on factory floors. Such “deployment” experience—and the data these robots gather—helps robots adapt to specific workplaces and tasks. Better foundational models make that site-specific data more valuable because robots can learn from it faster, Tedrake said.

Recent experiments have tested how much work a general-purpose model can do without specialized training on robotic data. Researchers gave Astra camera images, robot information and a control interface that allowed the model to command the robot to take certain actions. In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark—where the model commands a simulated robot in a digital simulation, as opposed to a real robot—compared with 51.0% reported by the best specialized robotic models on this leaderboard.

Shi said advances in general models’ spatial and reasoning capabilities already let them handle tasks that previously required dedicated training. They can cope when a bottle is in a different position or the lighting changes, and reason about the sequence of a task or which step went wrong, he said.

Meanwhile, large language models are powerful but slow and need to be hosted in the cloud, meaning the robot or device needs a constant network connection. Shi still sees a need for smaller, specialized models that can run on a robot’s onboard computer without needing a constant internet connection.

“There may be different starting points for how to grow intelligence,” Pete Florence, cofounder of Generalist, a startup training general-purpose AI models for robots, told Fortune. He said it was unclear that any existing model would be the one that dominates robotics in the long-run. For its part, OpenAI said it was reassigning its robotics researchers to other teams because it now believes this is the best way to accelerate progress towards building general-purpose robots.

Back at booth #208 at CoRL, a few former members of the once-unified, stand-alone OpenAI robotics team milled about. They still drew a crowd, despite having no display or demo. After all, one of the conference’s hottest questions was how much robotics expertise would remain valuable as general-purpose models grew more capable—and the experience of those former OpenAI robotics researchers, now dispatched to other teams, offered one answer. Update, Nov. 13: This story has been updated to clarify the status of the OpenAI robotics team members who were at CoRL.

Alpha School, the network of AI-driven private schools charging parents up to $75,000 a year, has won backers from Silicon Valley to the Trump administration. Its own data show most of its students aren’t reaching the model’s central promise.

Only 42% of Alpha students met the network’s goal of learning twice as fast in both math and reading, according to internal data first reported by The New York Times . The findings land as Alpha pushes into public schools, where districts are adopting its software in hopes of fitting more learning into less time.

## What Alpha promises parents

Alpha has no traditional teachers. It employs what it calls “guides,” whose job, according to the company’s marketing materials, is to “make every student feel valued and motivated.” Guides don’t plan lessons or grade homework, Fortune reported in September .

The core of the pitch is that students will “learn twice as much as their peers in two hours of academics a day” using TimeBack, an app Alpha markets as an AI tutor. Cofounder MacKenzie Price says the app personalizes and accelerates learning for each student, freeing the rest of the school day for workshops on skills such as public speaking and relationship building.

The network has grown fast. A spokesperson told Fortune in September that Alpha had more than 1,200 students. The Times put the figure at about 1,500 across roughly 50 campuses, in line with the expansion plans Alpha announced in August .

That pitch has drawn AI optimists. “I definitely think using AI well is a skill in the future, if not the skill, so it’s kind of a disservice not to have that in school,” Sarah Cone, a venture capitalist whose 8-year-old daughter attends Alpha’s New York campus, told Fortune in September.

In September 2025, U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon toured Alpha’s Austin campus and called its model “the most exciting thing I’ve seen in education in a long time.” LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman and hedge fund manager Bill Ackman have both publicly backed Price and Alpha on X. Even the X account of Elizabeth Holmes, the Theranos founder serving more than 11 years in prison for fraud, praised Price .

## Where students are falling short

Math is the bigger gap. About half of K-8 students at Alpha’s private campuses missed the goal of learning math twice as fast, and roughly one in five missed their reading targets, according to the Times ‘ review of the network’s data.

Students who started behind fared worse. About a fifth of Alpha’s private school students scored at or below the 50th percentile nationally in math last fall, and only 37% of that group met the network’s 2x growth goal by winter, the Times found.

The two-hour premise is also in question. Guides and parents told Wired that students worked late into the night to meet the school’s goals. One parent of a 13-year-old reading at an 11th-grade level said reaching those goals came with “stress and anxiety.”

Former employees told 404 Media that Alpha’s AI generated faulty lesson plans, which internal documents said sometimes did “more harm than good,” and that the company scraped other online courses without permission.

## Alpha’s model is reaching public schools

More than 2,600 public school students in Texas and South Carolina now use Alpha’s platform, according to company documents reviewed by the Times . That is a tougher test: public schools can’t remove struggling students, the Times noted, and they lack the prize incentives Alpha uses at its private campuses.

The Houston Independent School District, the largest in Texas, is piloting the software at two schools. Superintendent Mike Miles told the Times that students spent more time on Alpha’s apps than planned, cutting into other activities. He still wants AI in the district’s toolkit, calling it an important tool for students to be “successful in a different world and workplace.”

## Research points to a learning penalty

Alpha’s expansion comes as schools grapple with falling math and reading scores and growing evidence that how students use AI matters as much as whether they use it.

A study of 26,811 secondary students in central China found that homework scores rose 18% after students adopted generative AI tools, while closed-book exam scores fell 20%. The OECD’s latest PISA results found that daily AI users scored lower in science than nonusers, while moderate users performed about the same .

Professors have told Fortune that students who lean on AI summaries struggle with sustained reading. “Today, if you assign that amount of reading, they often don’t know what to do,” Timothy O’Malley, a theology professor at the University of Notre Dame, told Fortune ‘s Preston Fore in June .

“It’s not even an inability to critically think,” Jessica Hooten Wilson, a professor of great books and humanities at Pepperdine University, told Fortune . “It’s an inability to read sentences.”
